text: Australian Wheat Exports Set to Surge 47% Amid Black Sea Disruptions Australia is on track to export around 2.6 million tonnes of grain in October, 47% above the five-year average, as escalating attacks on Black Sea ships and grain terminals disrupt wheat supplies from Russia and Ukraine. Wheat is expected to account for roughly two-thirds of shipments, making this Australia's busiest October for grain exports in 16 years. Rising demand from the Philippines, Indonesia, China and other markets is boosting Australia's role in global grain trade. Meanwhile, wheat, soybean and corn futures edged higher, as traders monitor supply disruptions, export flows and geopolitical risks shaping agricultural commodity prices.

text: Europe’s Carmakers Get Temporary Relief From China Ahead of Paris Motor Show European automakers, including Volkswagen, Stellantis and Renault, have received a boost after China and the European Union reached an agreement in principle to reduce Chinese hybrid vehicle exports to the bloc by more than half. The move follows growing trade tensions and comes as European manufacturers struggle with declining sales, rising costs and increasing competition from Chinese brands. The Paris Motor Show, running from October 12 to 18, will showcase how European carmakers are responding with new electric vehicles, affordable models and strategic partnerships. However, Chinese manufacturers such as BYD, XPeng and Leapmotor continue to expand their presence, competing on price, technology and features. text: Russia to Ease Diesel Export Restrictions, Deputy PM Says Russia plans to gradually lift restrictions on diesel fuel exports, Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said on October 9, following US President Donald Trump’s announcement of a deal reached during a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin. Novak said Moscow welcomed US efforts to stabilise global energy markets and was ready to coordinate further measures to support predictable energy trade. According to Novak, Russia could supply the United States and other partners with 300,000 tonnes of diesel in October, 500,000 tonnes in November and up to 1 million tonnes in December, eventually reaching 3 million tonnes per month. He added that domestic demand would remain fully supplied. The announcement signals a potential increase in global diesel availability, although Russia’s government had previously extended its export restrictions through October 31.

text: EU Plans Measures to Halve Chinese Hybrid Car Imports The European Union is considering safeguard measures to reduce hybrid car imports from China by half, targeting approximately 400,000 vehicles annually compared with an estimated 800,000 in 2026. According to people familiar with the discussions, the measures could be introduced by December and may involve tariff-rate quotas, imposing additional duties on imports exceeding specified limits. EU trade chief Maroš Šefčovič said the proposal must still be discussed with member states, with the bloc aiming to ensure compliance with World Trade Organization rules. The proposed restrictions come amid growing concerns over China’s expanding automotive exports and Europe’s weakening industrial competitiveness. Chinese-made vehicles accounted for about a quarter of European hybrid sales in August, while European manufacturers such as Mercedes-Benz, Volkswagen and BMW face declining sales and profitability pressures. The EU-China understanding is expected to span four years and could serve as a model for addressing trade imbalances in other industries. However, the final mechanism and implementation details remain under discussion as both sides seek to balance domestic industry protection with stable trade relations.

text: Trump Calls Nobel Peace Prize Decision an “Indelible Stain” on Norway US President Donald Trump has criticized Norway after missing out on the Nobel Peace Prize, calling the decision an “indelible stain” on the country. Trump described this year’s winner, Navi Pillay, a prominent jurist and former UN human rights chief, as a “mystery person” and questioned her achievements in social media posts. The Norwegian Nobel Committee said Pillay was recognized for her efforts to promote peace and international law, including holding states and world leaders accountable. The controversy comes amid growing tensions between Washington and international legal institutions. Pillay has worked on major human rights cases, including investigations into the Rwandan genocide, and has criticized efforts to weaken international justice. The Trump administration also announced sanctions against the International Criminal Court, arguing that it threatens US sovereignty. The developments have renewed debate over the role of international law, the independence of the Nobel Committee and the relationship between political leadership and global accountability.
